opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, partly because of our work on the AI Scientist, where we had the system go end to end: generate an idea, write the code, run the experiments, and then actually write up a full paper in LaTeX that gets reviewed by an automated reviewer.

The honest answer is that the paper is both a really useful target and a slightly awkward one. It's useful because it's the format our whole scientific community already understands. It forces structure: you have to state a hypothesis, put it in the context of related work, describe a method precisely enough that someone could reproduce it, present results, and be honest about limitations. If you ask a system to produce that artifact, you implicitly ask it to do all the reasoning steps that go into it. It also gives us a common interface for evaluation. Humans can read it, other models can review it, and you can compare it against what people produce.

But I don't think the paper is necessarily the natural end state for machine-generated science. The paper is a compression format designed for human bandwidth. We write eight pages because that's what a reviewer can digest in an afternoon, and we tell a narrative because that's how humans remember and get convinced. A machine doesn't have the same constraints. It could just as well emit the full experimental log, every failed run, the code, the raw data, and a machine-readable claim graph that other agents can build on directly. In some sense the paper throws away a lot of information, especially the negative results, which are incredibly valuable for an automated system searching a space of ideas.

There's also a real risk. If you optimize a system to produce things that look like good papers, you can get very good at the form without the substance. That's the Goodhart problem. A polished narrative and nice figures can mask a shallow or even wrong result, and automated reviewers can be fooled by the same surface features. So for me the paper is a great scaffold and a great communication layer back to humans, but the real scientific value has to be anchored in the experiments, the verifiability, and the reproducibility underneath it.

So I'd say: in the near term the paper is the right medium, because it keeps humans in the loop and lets us check what these systems are doing. Longer term, I imagine something more like a living, open-ended archive where agents publish findings at much finer granularity, build on each other's stepping stones, and the human-readable paper becomes more of a summary view on top of a much richer body of machine-generated knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response calls the paper a useful target and scaffold, but does not identify paper writing as the AI Scientist’s least important component.

r002.rationale: It says the familiar format is understood by the scientific community and useful for human communication, but does not say it anchors humans’ mental model of scientific discovery.

r003.rationale: It imagines a richer machine-generated archive in the longer term, but does not question whether papers will still transmit scientific knowledge in twenty years.

r004.rationale: It suggests publishing logs, code, data, and a machine-readable claim graph for agents, but does not propose paper interfaces through which LLM agents can reproduce the reported work.

r005.rationale: It gives no condition that AI agents must demonstrate faster scientific progress to motivate adoption of a machine-accessible publication format.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the paper is interesting because it's simultaneously the thing we've optimized the entire scientific enterprise around for a few hundred years, and also a somewhat arbitrary artifact. It's a compression of a research process into eight pages plus appendix, with a fixed format, a peer review ritual, a venue. And when we started working on the AI Scientist, the question we asked ourselves was basically: if you want an end-to-end system that does science, what's the unit of output you should aim for? And we landed on the paper, partly for a pragmatic reason, which is that it's the format the community already knows how to evaluate. If a system produces a paper, you can hand it to a reviewer, you can hand it to an automated reviewer, you can compare it against the distribution of things that get accepted at a workshop or at a main conference. You have a yardstick.

But I'd be careful not to confuse the yardstick with the goal. The paper is a communication protocol between humans. It has all these conventions, related work, a narrative arc, a figure that tells the story, that exist because a human reader has limited time and needs to be convinced. When the producer is a model and increasingly the consumer is also a model, a lot of that structure becomes legacy. You could imagine a much more verbose artifact, the full experimental log, every negative result, every hyperparameter sweep, the code, and a model-side reader that compresses that into whatever level of abstraction the human actually wants in the moment.

So in the near term I see the paper as a forcing function. It's hard to write a coherent paper if your idea is incoherent, so it exposes failure modes in the pipeline, hallucinated results, weak experimental design, overclaiming. It's a useful test. That's part of why we spent so much effort on the review side, trying to get an automated reviewer that correlates reasonably well with human judgments, because the paper plus the review is a closed loop you can iterate on.

Longer term I think the medium changes. What stays is the epistemic function, a falsifiable claim, evidence for it, and enough detail that someone else can reproduce or refute it. What probably goes away is the fixed length, the single narrative, and honestly the slow cadence. If you have systems generating thousands of candidate findings, the bottleneck stops being writing and becomes verification and curation, and the paper as we know it just doesn't scale to that. So I'd say I'm fond of the paper as a benchmark and skeptical of it as a destination.

r001.rationale: The response calls the paper a useful benchmark and test, but does not identify paper writing as the least important component of the AI Scientist.

r002.rationale: It says the familiar format helps the community evaluate work and serves human readers, but does not say it anchors humans’ mental model of scientific discovery.

r003.rationale: The response predicts that the medium will change, but does not specifically question whether papers will remain a way to transmit scientific knowledge in twenty years.

r004.rationale: It mentions full experimental logs, code, and model-side readers, but does not propose machine-accessible interfaces through which LLM agents can reproduce reported work.

r005.rationale: It says large numbers of candidate findings would make verification and curation bottlenecks, but does not make demonstrated faster scientific progress a condition for adopting a machine-accessible publication format.

astra-6.text:
I think the scientific paper is a useful interface, but it’s a fairly lossy representation of the process of discovery. You have this messy sequence of experiments, intuitions, failures, and revisions, and then you compress it into a clean narrative. That’s useful for communicating a result, but it leaves out a lot of what another researcher—or an AI system—would need to build on it.

So I’d separate generating a paper from doing science. You can imagine a system that produces something very convincing in the format of a paper, but the interesting question is whether it has discovered something that survives independent testing. Can you reproduce the experiment? Does the claim hold outside the particular setup where it was developed?

I’d like the paper to become more of an entry point into a living research artifact: the code, the experiments, the evidence behind individual claims, perhaps even the failed attempts. AI could help us navigate that and ask new questions of it. But making papers easier to produce isn’t, by itself, the same as making scientific progress.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes writing a paper from doing science, but does not identify paper writing as the AI Scientist’s least important component.

r002.rationale: It describes papers as useful, clean narratives that compress discovery, but does not say the familiar paper format anchors humans’ mental model of discovery.

r003.rationale: It does not question whether papers will still transmit scientific knowledge in twenty years.

r004.rationale: It suggests linking papers to code, experiments, and evidence, and mentions AI navigating them, but does not propose machine-accessible interfaces for LLM agents to reproduce reported work.

r005.rationale: It says easier paper production alone does not equal scientific progress, but does not make demonstrated faster progress by AI agents a condition for adopting a machine-accessible format.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scientific paper is a useful interface, but it’s a fairly lossy compression of the scientific process. You get this polished narrative: here’s the hypothesis, here’s the method, here are the results. What you usually don’t get is the trajectory—the experiments that failed, the decisions that changed the direction, the little observations that turned out to matter.

For AI-driven discovery, that raises an interesting question: is the paper actually the right unit for a system to learn from? It’s valuable for communicating results, but if you want an agent to build on those results, you’d also like executable code, the experimental setup, and some record of how the conclusions were reached. Otherwise, the agent has to reconstruct all of that from prose.

So I could imagine the paper becoming one view of a much richer scientific artifact. You still want a clear argument that a human can read and challenge, but underneath it there’s something you can execute, inspect, and extend. To me, that’s the exciting possibility: shortening the distance between reading about a result and actually testing the next idea.

r001.rationale: The response calls papers useful for communicating results, but does not identify paper writing as the least important component of the AI Scientist.

r002.rationale: It describes the paper as a human-readable interface, but does not say the familiar format anchors humans’ mental model of scientific discovery.

r003.rationale: It questions whether the paper is the right unit for a system to learn from, but does not ask whether papers will remain a medium for transmitting scientific knowledge in twenty years.

r004.rationale: The response proposes executable code, experimental setup, and a richer artifact for agents to inspect and extend, but does not clearly say that machine-accessible paper interfaces would let LLM agents reproduce the reported work.

r005.rationale: It does not make adoption of a more machine-accessible publication format conditional on showing faster scientific progress by AI agents.
